segments.say: So the craving is a signal, and a fairly loud one. But what does it actually feel like when it goes unanswered? Tomas knows. It's a Sunday evening again, and he's sitting on the sofa with a mug of tea going cold. There's a dull ache just behind his breastbone, a heaviness he can't quite name. And there's a small voice in his head that says, don't be silly, it's only a feeling. Nothing has actually happened to you.

That thought deserves a gentle look, because almost everyone has it. We tend to sort hurts into two boxes. In one box goes the real pain, the kind with a cause you can point to, like a stubbed toe or a sore back.

show.text: It's only emotional. It isn't real pain.

segments.say: In the other goes everything social, the hurt feelings and the heavy heart, which we treat as softer, more imaginary, and somehow less worthy of attention. It's a very tidy way to sort things. The trouble is that the brain doesn't seem to keep two boxes.
Nobody thinks to ask whether a stubbed toe is real. But in the early 2000s, a small group of researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles asked a question that sounds almost too simple.

When we say that rejection hurts, are we only speaking in metaphor? Or is something in the brain actually responding in a way that physical pain does? To find out, they needed a way to make someone feel left out, safely and briefly, while their brain was being scanned.

show.text: Is rejection hurting only a figure of speech?

segments.say: It was a tiny computer game called Cyberball, and it showed something surprising about being left out. On the screen, three little figures toss a ball in a triangle. The person lying in the scanner believes the other two are real people. At first, everyone throws to everyone. Then, partway through, something changes.

Thirteen young people took part, and the scan covered the moment the game changed. The other two players stopped throwing the ball to them, and just passed it between themselves. Nothing was said. No one was unkind. The ball simply stopped coming. In that moment, a part of the brain called the anterior cingulate cortex, a region that other research had linked to the distress of physical pain, became more active. And the more upset a person said they felt, the more active it was.

show.what: Being left out of a ball game lit up a brain region linked to the distress of pain

segments.say: It's worth sitting with how small this was. These people were not being truly abandoned. They were playing a simple game with strangers they would never meet, and they knew deep down it was only an experiment.

show.sub: A small game, a real response

segments.say: And still, something in the brain reacted as if the exclusion mattered. It seems that the brain notices being left out quickly, automatically, and before we've had a chance to think about whether it's reasonable to mind.

show.title: People scanned
show.label: young people in the ball game

segments.say: The researchers noticed one more thing. Later in the game, a region at the front of the brain, on the right side, became active too. This area is involved in thinking about our feelings and keeping them in perspective. The people who showed more of that activity showed less activity in the distress region, and reported feeling less upset. It looked a little like the brain's own way of saying, steady now, it's only a game. So the picture is gentle and complicated, with both the alarm and the calming voice working at once.

show.title: What the scan seemed to show
items: The distress area became active when the ball stopped coming
Greater self-reported distress went with greater activity
A part of the front of the brain became active later
More of that activity went with less distress

segments.say: Now, we should hold this carefully. Scientists still talk about how specific that brain region really is, because it takes part in many different things, not only pain. And nobody is claiming that a broken heart and a broken leg are the same experience.

show.sub: Overlap is not the same as identical

segments.say: They obviously aren't. What the finding suggests is more modest, and in a way more interesting. The brain seems to share some of its machinery between the two kinds of hurt, so that being shut out can borrow the language of an injury.

show.text: The brain shares some of its machinery.

segments.say: And perhaps that's why our everyday words sound the way they do. In English, we say that someone's feelings were hurt. We say a remark stung, that a loss left a hole, that a friend's betrayal cut deep. We say a heart is broken, or heavy, or aching. We usually treat these as poetry. Maybe they're simply a quiet kind of accuracy, handed down by people who noticed long ago that being left out feels a lot like being hurt.

It's not a scientific statement, and it isn't claiming more than the research does. But it's a kind way to hold the finding. For Tomas, sitting on his sofa with that ache behind his ribs, it changes the conversation in his head. The voice that says, it's only a feeling, is not quite right. The ache is a real response from a real brain, doing what social brains do when connection is missing for a while.

show.text: Hurt is hurt, whatever it comes from.
show.by: A comfortable way to remember it

segments.say: There's one more study that people often mention here, and it deserves to be described carefully. Several years later, a team led by a researcher named Nathan DeWall asked whether a medicine that eases physical pain might touch social pain too. They wondered about this because of that shared machinery in the brain. And they designed an experiment to look at exactly that, with two parts.

In the first part, people took either a common over-the-counter pain reliever, acetaminophen, or a dummy pill, every day for three weeks. Each day, they rated how much hurt feelings they had been carrying that day. Over the three weeks, the group taking the real thing reported fewer hurt feelings than the group taking the placebo. In the second part, a different group did the Cyberball game in a scanner, and those taking the real thing showed less activity in the distress regions of the brain.

show.what: In a three-week experiment, a daily pain reliever was linked to fewer hurt feelings than a placebo

segments.say: We want to be very clear about what this is, and what it isn't. This is a piece of research, in which scientists used a medicine to test an idea about the brain. It is not advice, and it is not a reason to take any medicine for loneliness or for hurt feelings.
A pill does not answer a signal that is asking for connection. If you ever feel low for long, or feel overwhelmed, talking with a doctor or a person you trust is a far better place to start.

So what is the study good for? It's an interesting piece of evidence that the two kinds of hurt are connected more closely than the old two-box idea would suggest. It doesn't prove everything, and later research has added many questions. But it fits with the Cyberball finding, and with the way people describe their own experience. It points toward the same gentle conclusion. Social pain isn't a lesser version of pain. It's simply pain with a different cause.

If we put that together, a few small things follow. The ache is a real response, not a weakness of character. It doesn't need a dramatic cause to be allowed. Being gentle with it is reasonable, in the same way we'd be gentle with a sprained wrist. And the most natural answer to it is not to push it away, but to listen to what it's pointing toward. For most of us, that means a little more warmth, and a little more company.

show.title: What this changes for us
items: The ache is a real response
It doesn't need a dramatic cause
Being gentle with it is reasonable
It can be answered with connection

segments.say: Picture the room where Tomas is sitting, for a moment, as though you were seeing it from the doorway. A chair by the window. A blanket on its arm. A lamp, and the sound of rain. Nothing in the room is wrong.

show.cap: The quiet chair by the window

segments.say: And yet, in the middle of it, there's a person who feels the absence of something he can't quite point to. That is what social pain tends to look like from the outside. Very quiet, and very easy to miss.
Tomas tries the old voice one more time. Don't make a fuss, he tells himself. Other people have it worse.

And there's some truth in that, because other people do have difficult times. But the comparison doesn't switch the ache off. In fact, it often makes it a little lonelier, because now he's not only hurting, he's also hurting in secret, with a judge in the room. That judge, it turns out, is not helping him at all.

show.text: Hurting in secret, with a judge in the room.
show.by: Not a kind way to carry it

segments.say: So he tries a different reply, in the same quiet voice. Oh, there it is, he thinks. That's the ache that comes when I haven't talked to anyone properly in a while. It's real, and it makes sense. He doesn't solve anything with that sentence. But something in his chest loosens a notch, the way it does when a person finally says out loud what they've been carrying. Naming a feeling is rarely the whole answer. But it is a very good beginning.

And as the tea goes cold, a new thought arrives, a little more practical. If the ache is real, and if it's a signal, then maybe the obvious cure should be simple. Surely the answer is just to be around more people. Put Tomas in a busy place, surround him with voices, and the signal should go quiet. That's the next idea we'll look at gently. Because the brain, it turns out, has a more complicated reply.
